main.title: Ecco: The Tides of Time
main.subtitle: Another journey through the ocean
main.summary: Ecco: The Tides of Time is Novotrade's underwater adventure, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 26 August 1994.

cards.heading: Another journey through the ocean
cards.text: Ecco: The Tides of Time is Novotrade's underwater adventure, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 26 August 1994. Ecco returns to a world of ocean passages, unfamiliar creatures and threats connected to the Vortex. Swimming and exploration remain central, with air and health requiring attention as the dolphin searches for a route. The story also carries him into the future, where his descendant Trellia introduces another vision of life in the water. Travelling through time lets the sequel change the shape of the ocean itself.

cards.heading: Listening for a route
cards.text: Sonar serves several purposes. Ecco uses it to communicate, interact with special objects and inspect the surrounding area, while a charging attack lets him strike enemies and break through obstacles. Combining sonar with a charge extends his offensive reach. Some passages ask him to follow other dolphins through a maze; others involve collecting the scattered globes of the Asterite. Returning to the surface for air keeps exploration connected to the environment, so finding a promising opening also means judging whether Ecco can safely reach and investigate it.

cards.heading: Waterways through time
cards.text: Certain stages change Ecco's form, giving him the abilities of another creature for a particular task. Other sequences use a forward-moving perspective in which he passes through rings. The future introduces aerial waterways, extending the familiar act of swimming into spaces that seem impossible in the earlier ocean. These changes build variety around Ecco's movement rather than replacing it with an unrelated adventure. The Mega Drive music by Attila Dobos, András Magyari and Andy Armer supports a world whose beauty and unfamiliar sounds can make even a quiet passage feel uncertain.

main.title: EarthBound
main.summary: EarthBound, released in Japan as Mother 2, is a 1994 role-playing game developed by Ape Inc. and HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.heading: EarthBound
cards.text: EarthBound, originally released in Japan as Mother 2: Gīgu no Gyakushū, is a 1994 role-playing video game developed by Ape Inc. (now Creatures Inc.) and HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. The second entry in the Mother series, it follows a young boy named Ness and his party of Paula, Jeff and Poo, as they travel the world to collect melodies from eight Sanctuaries to defeat the universal cosmic destroyer Giygas.

cards.heading: Itoi, Iwata and five-year development
cards.text: EarthBound had a lengthy development period that spanned five years. Its returning staff from EarthBound Beginnings (1989) included writer/director Shigesato Itoi and lead programmer Satoru Iwata, as well as composers Keiichi Suzuki and Hirokazu Tanaka, who incorporated a diverse range of styles into the soundtrack, including salsa, reggae, and dub. Most of the other staff members had not worked on the original EarthBound Beginnings, and the game came under repeated threats of cancellation until Iwata joined the team. Originally scheduled for release in January 1993, the game was completed around May 1994 and first released in Japan in August 1994, and in North America in June 1995. A port for the Game Boy Advance developed by Pax Softnica, bundled with Mother, as Mother 1 + 2, was released only in Japan in 2003.

cards.heading: The design
cards.text: Like its predecessor, EarthBound is themed around an idiosyncratic portrayal of Americana and Western culture, subverting popular role-playing game traditions by featuring a modern setting while parodying numerous staples of the genre. Itoi wanted the game to reach non-gamers with its intentionally goofy tone; for example, the player uses items such as the Pencil Eraser to remove pencil statues (octopus statues in the Japanese version), experiences in-game hallucinations, and battles piles of vomit, taxi cabs, and walking nooses. For its American release, the game was marketed with a $2 million promotional campaign that sardonically proclaimed: "This game stinks." The game's puns and humor were reworked by localizer Marcus Lindblom. Since the original Mother had not yet been released outside Japan on the Nintendo Entertainment System before 2015, Mother 2 was called EarthBound to avoid confusion about what it was a sequel to.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: Although it was positively received by Japanese audiences, EarthBound sold quite poorly in the United States. Journalists attributed the game's poor sales in the West to a combination of its simple graphics, satirical marketing campaign, and a lack of market interest in the genre. In the ensuing years, a dedicated fan community spawned that advocated for the series' recognition, particularly after Ness appeared as a playable character in the Super Smash Bros. series. By the 2000s, multiple reader polls and critics had named it one of the greatest video games of all time, and it became regarded as a "sacred cow among gaming's cognoscenti". It was followed by the Japan-only sequel Mother 3 for the Game Boy Advance in 2006. EarthBound was later made available worldwide on the Wii U Virtual Console in 2013, 3DS Virtual Console in 2016, the SNES Classic in 2017, and the Nintendo Classics service in February 2022.

main.title: Virtua Cop
main.summary: A shrinking target gives each gunman a deadline, turning a moving polygonal crime scene into a test of attention and accurate shooting.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Virtua Cop is Sega AM2's 1994 Model 2 arcade light-gun shooter, brought to Saturn in 1995. One or two police officers move through three stages of a criminal investigation as the game controls the camera. Polygonal locations and animated opponents let threats appear from behind objects, around corners and at different distances within the same scene.

cards.heading: Read the threat before firing
cards.text: An enemy's target marker changes colour as the moment to fire approaches. The signal gives the player a way to judge which gunman needs attention first when several appear together. A civilian can enter the same space, turning a quick reaction into a judgement about what the gun is pointing at. The moving camera keeps replacing one arrangement with another. Learning the stage means remembering dangerous entrances, then placing the shot accurately enough to avoid harming someone who needs protection.

cards.heading: Make room to reload
cards.text: The handgun holds a limited number of shots and reloads when the player fires away from the screen. Emptying it at the wrong moment leaves an immediate problem, so a short gap between enemies becomes valuable. Other weapons offer more firepower, but their ammunition or continued possession is limited. Choosing when to reload and when to spend a special weapon gives the shooting a rhythm beyond pulling the trigger as quickly as possible.

cards.heading: Aim for more than survival
cards.text: Shooting an enemy's weapon can earn a Justice Shot, while accurate sequences build the score multiplier. Surviving a scene is therefore only the first target. A player who knows where the next gunman will appear can aim for a more exact hit and protect a growing sequence of successful shots. That scoring layer gives the same route another purpose on a return visit: the danger is familiar, but the quality and order of the shots can still improve.

main.title: Live A Live
main.subtitle: An RPG told across seven eras
main.summary: Square released Live A Live in Japan for the Super Famicom on September 2, 1994.

cards.heading: Seven eras, seven beginnings
cards.text: Square released Live A Live in Japan for the Super Famicom on September 2, 1994. Directed by Takashi Tokita, it offers seven stories set in different eras, each with its own protagonist, tone and rules. Players can move from a western town to feudal Japan or a distant-future spacecraft. A shared grid-based battle system connects the episodes, while their situations give each one a different pace.

cards.heading: An anthology of adventures
cards.text: The opening scenarios cover prehistory, imperial China, feudal Japan, the Wild West, the present day, the near future and the distant future. Each introduces a new cast and setting. Recurring systems and motifs gradually connect these short adventures, allowing the player to discover how they belong within a larger story. The anthology structure gives individual episodes room for their own mysteries, jokes and dramatic turns.

cards.heading: Different objectives, shared battles
cards.text: In the Wild West chapter, preparing traps is part of organising a town's defence. Feudal Japan offers opportunities for stealth, the distant future emphasises exploration and tension, and the present-day scenario is built around a series of fights. These changes make the common battle system serve different objectives. The player repeatedly has to learn what matters in the current situation, even after becoming familiar with combat.

cards.heading: A wider audience in 2022
cards.text: The original remained closely associated with Japan and the Super Famicom for many years. In 2022, an internationally released remake presented its stories with HD-2D graphics. That new edition brought the anthology to a wider audience while retaining its distinct episodes and their different approaches to the role-playing game. Its return renewed attention to the structure Tokita and Square had developed in 1994.

main.title: Contra: Hard Corps
main.subtitle: A different soldier, a different barrage
main.summary: Konami’s Mega Drive Contra gives four fighters distinct weapons and sends their campaign along branching routes.

cards.heading: A new task force
cards.text: Contra: Hard Corps is Konami’s side-scrolling run-and-gun game, first released for Genesis in North America on 14 September 1994. A new task force confronts Colonel Bahamut after the theft of an alien cell intended for use in weapons. The player chooses from four distinct soldiers, each bringing a different selection of guns into the campaign. Two players can fight together with different characters. Running and jumping quickly lead into large enemy encounters, making the opening stages a succession of threats that demand attention to both movement and fire.

cards.heading: Holding a position under fire
cards.text: The firing controls offer two useful relationships between aiming and movement. One lets the character move while shooting; the other holds the soldier in place while the player aims in different directions. Switching between them changes whether a dangerous pattern is best answered by retreating or by staying still to hit a particular target. Each character’s weapon set further changes that decision. A familiar enemy can therefore demand a different position when approached with another fighter, giving the choice at the start of the game lasting consequences.

cards.heading: The road divides
cards.text: Decisions during the story can lead to different routes and endings, so clearing one path leaves other encounters to discover. Brief scenes connect the battles and present those choices without taking the action away from its side-on perspective. In Europe and Australia the game appeared as Probotector, with altered characters. The branching structure and four weapon sets make returning to the campaign more than a search for a cleaner performance along a single fixed route.

entries.factual_note: One entry for the first original release; later regional editions and ports are discussed within the same historical article.

main.title: Kirby’s Dream Course
main.subtitle: Kirby becomes the ball
main.summary: Kirby’s Dream Course began on Japan’s Super Famicom on September 21, 1994, under the name Kirby Bowl. HAL Laboratory turns Kirby into the ball in a golf-like game of raised platforms, sloping ground and carefully judged shots. Enemies stand where a conventional course would offer a clear route to the cup. Hitting them changes the playing field. When only one enemy remains, it becomes the cup needed to finish.

cards.heading: Kirby becomes the ball
cards.text: Kirby’s Dream Course began on Japan’s Super Famicom on September 21, 1994, under the name Kirby Bowl. HAL Laboratory turns Kirby into the ball in a golf-like game of raised platforms, sloping ground and carefully judged shots. Enemies stand where a conventional course would offer a clear route to the cup. Hitting them changes the playing field. When only one enemy remains, it becomes the cup needed to finish.

cards.heading: Reading the ground before the shot
cards.text: Direction, power and spin matter as much as the destination. A shot can roll along the ground or send Kirby through the air, while copied powers provide another way to negotiate a hazard. A parasol lets him float, ice can freeze water and fire changes how he tackles opponents. The isometric view encourages players to read the course before acting: a slope, conveyor belt or trampoline can turn an apparent obstacle into part of the route.

cards.heading: A course for two rivals
cards.text: The game also supports two-player competition, so the same compact courses become a contest between opponents rather than a solitary puzzle. Its eight regular courses give a familiar character a different physical vocabulary, built from angles and momentum instead of running and jumping. Later Virtual Console editions and the SNES Classic rereleased this original game. The unusual blend of golf, puzzle-solving and copied powers remains at the centre of that experience.

main.title: System Shock
main.summary: System Shock is a 1994 first-person action-adventure video game developed by LookingGlass Technologies and published by Origin Systems.

cards.heading: System Shock
cards.text: System Shock is a 1994 first-person action-adventure video game developed by LookingGlass Technologies and published by Origin Systems. It was directed by Doug Church with Warren Spector serving as producer. The game is set aboard a space station in a cyberpunk vision of the year 2072. Assuming the role of a nameless security hacker, the player attempts to hinder the plans of a malevolent artificial intelligence called SHODAN.

cards.heading: Physics and emergent play converge
cards.text: System Shock's 3D engine, physics simulation and complex gameplay have been cited as both innovative and influential. The developers sought to build on the emergent gameplay and immersive environments of their previous games, Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss and Ultima Underworld II: Labyrinth of Worlds, by streamlining their mechanics into a more "integrated whole"; it is considered one of the defining examples of an immersive sim.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: Critics praised System Shock and hailed it as a major breakthrough in its genre. It was later placed on multiple hall of fame lists. The game was a moderate commercial success, with sales exceeding 170,000 copies, but Looking Glass ultimately lost money on the project. A sequel, System Shock 2, was released by Looking Glass Studios and offshoot developer Irrational Games in 1999. The 2000 game Deus Ex (produced and directed by Spector), the 2007 game BioShock, and the 2017 game Prey are spiritual successors to the two games. A remake by Nightdive Studios was released on May 30, 2023.

main.title: Earthworm Jim
main.summary: Earthworm Jim is a 1994 run and gun video game developed by Shiny Entertainment and published by Playmates Interactive Entertainment. The game was released for the Sega Genesis and Super Nintendo Entertainment System, before being subsequently ported to several other video game consoles.

cards.heading: An earthworm becomes a hero
cards.text: Earthworm Jim is a 1994 run and gun video game developed by Shiny Entertainment and published by Playmates Interactive Entertainment. The game was released for the Sega Genesis and Super Nintendo Entertainment System, before being subsequently ported to several other video game consoles.

cards.heading: A blaster, a whip and Peter Puppy
cards.text: The game plays as a 2D sidescrolling platformer with elements of a run and gun game as well. The player controls Jim and must maneuver him through the level while avoiding obstacles and enemies. The player can use Jim's gun as a method of shooting enemies, or his worm body as a whip for whipping enemies. The whip move also allows the player to grab hold of, and swing from, certain hooks. Some levels have additional requirements beyond merely getting to the end of the level. For example, the level "For Pete's Sake" involves making sure the computer-controlled Peter Puppy character gets through the level unscathed, which is accomplished by whipping him to make him jump over pits, and defeating enemies before they can harm him. Failure to do so results in Peter lashing out at Jim, depleting his health.

cards.heading: Racing through Andy Asteroids
cards.text: In between most levels, a racing level called "Andy Asteroids" is played. Unlike the rest of the game, it places the viewpoint behind Jim. The player must direct Jim on his rocket, in a race against Psy-Crow, through a tube-like structure while collecting items and boosts and avoiding asteroids. If the player wins, the next level is started instantly. If Psy-Crow wins, a boss fight against him must be won to progress to the next level.

cards.heading: The super suit and its enemies
cards.text: Jim is a normal earthworm, until a special "super suit" falls from the sky and allows him to operate much like a human, with his worm body acting as a head and the suit acting as a body. Jim now must evade the game's many antagonists, who want the suit back. The game plays out with Jim succeeding in his quest to meet Princess What's-Her-Name. However, she is crushed by a cow that Jim launched into space at the beginning of the game.

cards.heading: A sketch becomes a new franchise
cards.text: Playmates Toys, finding success with the license for Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, wanted to start their own franchise. Inspired by the success of the Sonic the Hedgehog series with its first and second installments, they decided that they wanted to start the franchise as a video game, a rare approach at the time. From there, the game's design actually started with Douglas TenNapel's simple sketch of an earthworm that he presented to Shiny Entertainment. Programmer David Perry and the rest of Shiny bought the rights to Earthworm Jim from TenNapel and started developing the game. From there, TenNapel would work on doing the game design, making level ideas, and voicing Jim's character, while Perry and the other programmers created additional characters and game mechanics. Perry recounted that the giant hamster "was drawn by one of our guys at three o'clock one morning".

cards.heading: Building two console versions
cards.text: The game was developed simultaneously for the Genesis and Super NES using a "custom heterogeneous programming language" created by Shiny Entertainment. Almost all levels were first programmed by Dave Perry on the Genesis and then converted to the Super NES by Nick Jones. "For Pete's Sake" was coded simultaneously on both platforms by Andy Astor, and "Andy Asteroids" and "Snot a Problem" were originally programmed on the Super NES by Nick Jones and then converted to the Genesis.

main.title: DOOM II
main.summary: Doom II, also known as Doom II: Hell on Earth, is a 1994 first-person shooter video game developed and published by id Software for MS-DOS. It was released on Mac OS the following year. Whereas the original Doom was initially only available through shareware and mail order, Doom II was the first Doom game released initially in stores.

cards.heading: Hell reaches Earth
cards.text: Doom II, also known as Doom II: Hell on Earth, is a 1994 first-person shooter video game developed and published by id Software for MS-DOS. It was released on Mac OS the following year. Whereas the original Doom was initially only available through shareware and mail order, Doom II was the first Doom game released initially in stores.

cards.heading: Exploring larger nonlinear levels
cards.text: Doom II reused the first game's engine to build larger, more intricate levels with bigger groups of monsters. Players explore nonlinear maps, collect weapons and search for a switch or teleporter leading to the next area. Detours can reveal health pickups and more powerful weapons. The scale and complexity of these maps also raised the computer requirements compared with the original game.

cards.heading: A continuous thirty-two-level campaign
cards.text: The campaign runs through 32 levels, including two secret stages reached from level 15. Its three sections take the player through Outpost, City and Hell, with short interludes advancing the story. Weapons and other inventory carry through the campaign. Between stages, a background replaces the episode maps used by the first Doom.

cards.heading: The Super Shotgun and new demons
cards.text: Doom II doubled the number of non-boss monster types and started using bosses from the original Doom as normal level enemies, in addition to adding a new weapon, the Super Shotgun (a very powerful double-barreled shotgun), and a new power-up, the Megasphere.

cards.heading: Designing the levels
cards.text: Most of the levels were designed by Sandy Petersen, with American McGee playing a significant role as well.

cards.heading: Bringing DOOM II to stores
cards.text: Doom II was released for DOS on October 10, 1994 in North America and Europe; distribution was handled by GT Interactive.

main.title: Sonic & Knuckles
main.subtitle: Two routes across Angel Island
main.summary: Sonic & Knuckles is Sonic Team's platform adventure, released for Mega Drive on 18 October 1994.

cards.heading: Two routes across Angel Island
cards.text: Sonic & Knuckles is Sonic Team's platform adventure, released for Mega Drive on 18 October 1994. Sonic pursues Doctor Robotnik and the Death Egg, while Knuckles faces a separate threat from EggRobo on Angel Island. Both characters run through zones filled with rings, springs and enemies, but their routes make different demands on the player. The game followed Sonic the Hedgehog 3 after the two projects had originally been planned together. Its cartridge also carried an unusual physical feature: a hinged slot for inserting another game.

cards.heading: A different way to climb
cards.text: Sonic jumps higher and uses the abilities associated with the elemental shields. Knuckles trades that reach for gliding and climbing, allowing him to cross openings and scale walls that change the shape of his route. Those differences extend to the encounters and passages each character faces. A familiar-looking stretch can therefore require another approach when replayed with Knuckles. Maintaining speed remains useful, but choosing where to jump, glide or climb makes the landscape a set of possibilities rather than a single shared race to the exit.

cards.heading: A cartridge that opens
cards.text: Connecting Sonic the Hedgehog 3 through the lock-on slot joins the two adventures into Sonic 3 & Knuckles, with their zones forming a longer journey. Connecting Sonic the Hedgehog 2 instead makes Knuckles playable in that earlier game. Other cartridges can lead to the Blue Sphere special-stage game. The connector turns a piece of cartridge hardware into part of the game's identity: an owner can place an existing game on top and discover a new use for it, with the combined third adventure offering the fullest version of the original plan.
